title: Reply to the Letter to the Editor regarding ‘Chi-squared and P-values vs. machine learning feature selection by Y. Takefuji’
abstract: We want to thank Dr. Takefuji for his interest in our publication ‘Development and validation of artificial intelligence-assisted transcriptomic signatures to personalize adjuvant chemotherapy in patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma’.1 Dr. Takefuji argues that using the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) and random forest (RF) for feature selection is not ideal because they do not provide true associations, and he proposes the use of chi-square tests and P values to ensure statistical significance in the associations between features and the target variable.2 We want to emphasize that developing a predictive model is a complex task that requires multiple dimensions to evaluate. The final results rely on the nature of the predictor and outcome variables. Moreover, certain tissues, such as stroma and immune cells, are frequently present in many of the samples, which could affect the final prediction in tumor-derived samples from patients. Therefore oversimplifying the predictive model development task by focusing only on the feature selection without a clear understanding of the types of variables in the analysis and the applied pipeline could generate methodological misinterpretation. It is crucial to consider various factors in predictive model development to ensure a comprehensive approach.

title: Artificial intelligence entering the pathology arena in oncology: current applications and future perspectives
abstract: BACKGROUND: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming the fields of pathology and oncology, offering novel opportunities for advancing diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment of cancer. METHODS: Through a systematic review-based approach, the representatives from the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) Precision Oncology Working Group (POWG) and international experts identified studies in pathology and oncology that applied AI-based algorithms for tumour diagnosis, molecular biomarker detection, and cancer prognosis assessment. These findings were synthesised to provide a comprehensive overview of current AI applications and future directions in cancer pathology. RESULTS: The integration of AI tools in digital pathology is markedly improving the accuracy and efficiency of image analysis, allowing for automated tumour detection and classification, identification of prognostic molecular biomarkers, and prediction of treatment response and patient outcomes. Several barriers for the adoption of AI in clinical workflows, such as data availability, explainability, and regulatory considerations, still persist. There are currently no prognostic or predictive AI-based biomarkers supported by level IA or IB evidence. The ongoing advancements in AI algorithms, particularly foundation models, generalist models and transformer-based deep learning, offer immense promise for the future of cancer research and care. AI is also facilitating the integration of multi-omics data, leading to more precise patient stratification and personalised treatment strategies. CONCLUSIONS: The application of AI in pathology is poised to not only enhance the accuracy and efficiency of cancer diagnosis and prognosis but also facilitate the development of personalised treatment strategies. Although barriers to implementation remain, ongoing research and development in this field coupled with addressing ethical and regulatory considerations will likely lead to a future where AI plays an integral role in cancer management and precision medicine. The continued evolution and adoption of AI in pathology and oncology are anticipated to reshape the landscape of cancer care, heralding a new era of precision medicine and improved patient outcomes.

title: 203eP Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) biomarkers and AI models for early detection of liver cancer: A systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract:
Background
Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common primary liver cancer and a significant global health burden. Emerging biomarkers such as cell-free DNA (cfDNA) have shown promise in non-invasive detection and diagnosis of HCC. This review aims to elucidate the value of cfDNA and AI-dependent models in assisting clinical diagnosis and treatment of HCC.
Methods
This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with the guidelines of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses of Diagnostic Test Accuracy Studies (PRISMA-DTA). A comprehensive literature search was conducted to include studies evaluating the diagnostic role of cfDNA in detection of HCC vs healthy or non-HCC controls in 4 databases: Embase, MEDLINE, Web of Science, and CENTRAL. The review protocol was registered with the PROSPERO International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (registration ID: CRD42024479037). Data analysis was conducted in R employing a random-effects model.
Results
A total of 27 studies with 12,004 patients were included for quantitative analysis. Pooled sensitivity of all studies was 87% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.82–0.92), while studies with healthy controls had a sensitivity of 87% (95% CI: 0.80–0.95). Pooled specificity was 89% (95% CI: 0.85–0.94), with the healthy controls group at 93% (95% CI: 0.88–0.98). Area-under curve (AUC) across all studies was 0.87 (95% CI: 0.84–0.94), with healthy group at 0.90 (95% CI: 0.85–0.95), suggesting good performance of models in diagnosing HCC via cfDNA.
Conclusions
Our analysis demonstrates high performance of models for diagnosing HCC, with better accuracy seen in diagnosing HCC from healthy controls. These findings suggest the potential of cfDNA as an emerging screening marker. Further studies are needed to validate our findings.

title: 1758eP An advanced cell-free DNA assay for prostate cancer early detection established by machine learning algorithm using whole-genome sequencing fragmentomic features
abstract:
Background
Early detection of prostate cancer is challenged by the limited specificity of prostate-specific antigen (PSA)-based screening. Circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA) fragmentomics may offer a promising non-invasive approach to improve screening accuracy and risk stratification.
Methods
This study retrospectively enrolled 106 patients with prostate cancer and 114 high-risk non-cancer individuals (training cohort) to develop a fragmentomics-based cfDNA assay for prostate cancer screening via plasma whole-genome sequencing. The fragmentomic features of copy number variant and fragmentation size profile were involved in machine learning algorithms for model training, followed by performance assessment in an independent cohort (validation cohort) including 83 cancer patients and 76 non-cancer individuals. We further combined the cfDNA assay with PSA to establish an integrated algorithm and evaluated its performance.
Results
The fragmentomics-based algorithm achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.939 (66.0% sensitivity at 95.6% specificity; 51.9% sensitivity at 98.2% specificity) when distinguishing cancer from non-cancer samples in the training cohort, with good calibration (slope, 1.371; intercept, -0.036). Similar discrimination was observed in the validation cohort using the threshold fixed in the training cohort (57.8% sensitivity at 92.1% specificity; AUC, 0.887), exhibiting a trend of elevating predictive probabilities (p=0.058) and decreased sensitivity (I, 27.3%; II, 55.3%; III, 68.0%; IV, 77.8%) across increased disease stages. Notably, the fragmentomics-based assay demonstrated outstanding performance within individuals having PSA between 4 and 10 ng/mL (AUC, 0.865; 69.0% sensitivity at 81.8% specificity). The integrated algorithm had higher AUC (0.915) and sensitivity at 98% specificity (I, 30.0%; II, 66.7%; III, 76.0%; IV, 87.5%) within the validation cohort.
Conclusions
We developed an advanced cfDNA assay utilizing plasma cfDNA fragmentomic features, which reached high accuracy for prostate cancer early detection, offering a promising tool in clinical practice.

title: 1889P AI-powered analysis of serum proteomics for forecasting immune-related adverse events (irAEs) in immunotherapy-treated NSCLC
abstract:
Background
Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) improved outcomes in NSCLC treatment, but caused immune-related adverse events (irAEs). Serum proteomic biomarkers combined with clinical data may offer a better approach for toxicity risk prediction.
Methods
To predict any irAE or severe (CTCAE grade 3-4) irAE, pre-treatment blood was collected from 162 NSCLC patients receiving ICIs. Serum proteins were profiled by high-resolution liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry, log-ratio–normalized, and dimensionally reduced. Five machine-learning algorithms-SVM, XGBoost, and other models- were evaluated using stratified 5-fold cross-validation with AUC. Kaplan–Meier analysis, log-rank testing, HR, and C-index were used for risk-stratification.
Results
The cohort (N=162) had a median age of 70.7 years, 50.9% were female, and 66.5% had adenocarcinoma. Baseline smoking status was 16.2% never, 68.2% former, and 15.0% current. Median TMB was 5.4 mut/Mb, and 58.1% were PD-L1 positive. Treatment included mono-ICI (35.3%), dual ICI (12.7%), or ICI + chemotherapy (52.0%), with 91.3% receiving palliative treatment. Overall, 54 patients (33.3%) experienced any irAE, and 32 (19.8%) developed severe irAEs. Frequent toxicities included pneumonitis (18.5%), rash (16.7%), and thyroiditis (14.8%). The model predicting any irAE yielded an AUC of 0.597 (95% CI 0.52-0.68). An optimized model for severe irAE prediction achieved an AUC of 0.695 (95% CI 0.57-0.81). This severe irAE model significantly stratified risk, with high-risk group (35% event rate) vs. the low-risk group (12% event rate) with HR 2.87, 95% CI 1.42-5.82; p=0.0022; C-index 0.622.
Conclusions
AI-driven serum-proteomic classifiers provide early, individualized forecasts of overall and severe irAEs. Although discrimination for any irAE was modest, severe-toxicity prediction nearly tripled hazard in high-risk patients, supporting proactive monitoring and pre-emptive management. These findings underscore the model’s clinical promise for risk assessment, and a planned prospective multi-center validation—coupled with the integration of genomic and radiomic data—will further boost accuracy and facilitate bedside adoption.

title: 121P Using AI-generated molecular digital twins to predict chemotherapy response in cancer
abstract:
Background
Predicting chemotherapy response is difficult and there are no widely accepted biomarkers routinely used in the clinic despite the success of precision medicine. A molecular Digital Twin is a virtual replication of an actual individual and their cancer which is AI-generated. We developed this novel modelling approach which evolved from astrophysics where advanced Bayesian inference enable integrative modelling of gravitational lensing, which we modified and applied to cancer biology. This novel technology combines tumour biology with clinical data to generate treatment predictions for multiple different chemotherapies such as anthracyclines and taxanes before the treatment is administered to help select the best therapeutic option.
Methods
Initially the model was trained on pre-clinical (CCLE and CTRP datasets) and clinical data (TCGA and BeatAML) from >11,000 patients with >20 cancer types, solid or haematological, treated with multiple different therapies. We present data for Digital Twin model prediction accuracies across solid tumours for predicting individualised treatment response and overall survival. This includes breast, lung, gliomas, ovary, pancreas and acute myeloid leukaemia.
Results

Table: 121P.

AUC ROC	Accuracy	Precision	Recall	Average Precision	AUC ROC	C-index	Brier score
84.9%	77.9%	80.4%	83.9%	88.5%	79.3%	76.0%	16.2%
Digital Twin accuracies Digital Twins are digital biomarkers which improve both drug response rates and overall survival. Retrospective analyses of TCGA dataset highlighted a doubling of median overall survival from 4.0 years, (95% CI: 3.7, 4.2) to 9.2 years (95% CI: 7.8, 15.2) when patients with cancer received treatment that was predicted by Digital Twin to be the best treatment for them versus those who received an alternative approved “standard of care”.
Conclusions
In conclusion, molecular Digital Twin predictions of therapeutic response can accurately select optimal cancer treatments for existing therapies at an individual level. With further clinical validation, applications of this technology has the potential to transform therapeutic development and clinical practise.

title: 184eP Detecting and monitoring low-abundance circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) by ultra-deep sequencing and machine learning
abstract:
Background
Detecting rare ctDNA variants in blood is a powerful tool for cancer diagnosis and treatment monitoring. However, this approach faces challenges from technical artifacts and biological confounders, especially when the tumor component is low.
Methods
To develop an ultra-deep version of targeted sequencing for low-ctDNA scenarios, blood samples were collected from non-cancer controls and patients with various cancer types as part of a preplanned substudy (NCT04972201). Plasma cfDNA (20–60 ng) and WBC genomic DNA(100ng) were processed using an enhanced UMI-tagging method and enriched with targeting panels for 168 and/or 520 cancer-related genes. The libraries were sequenced on the NovaSeq6000 platform to achieve a raw sequencing depth of 35,000–50,000X, resulting in a median unique depth of 4,000-4,500X. The data processing pipeline incorporated the following steps to suppress technical and biological noise. 1) Reads with identical UMIs and endpoint positions were used to collapse and merge to high-accuracy consensus sequences to eliminate pervasive random PCR and sequencing errors. 2) A deep-learning based noise model was trained to identify recurrent artifacts, such as DNA damage patterns and sequencer-specific error profiles. 3) To distinguish true somatic mutations from non-cancer biological aberrations (e.g. clonal hematopoiesis), paired WBC-sequencing was applied.
Results
Analytical sensitivity was evaluated using a dilution series across different tumor allele fraction (TAF) levels. The median limit of detection (LoD) is 0.25% with a 20 ng input and can reach as low as 0.15% with a 50 ng input. The limit of blank(LoB) was determined in 60 age-matched cancer-free donors, yielding an error rate of 1.1 × 10-7 across the entire panel. A combined precision and accuracy study was conducted using 302 samples from non-cancer donors and patients with seven cancer types, showing a positive percent agreement (PPA) of 87.8% for panel-wide SNVs, 94.0% for panel-wide indels, and a negative percent agreement (NPA) of >99.9%.
Conclusions
The advanced ultra-deep mutation sequencing technologies, combined with machine-learning tools offers a patient-care-ready liquid biopsy for variant-detection even at low tumor burden.

title: 186eP A random forest model to predict the type of pulmonary nodule based on DNA methylation sequencing data
abstract:
Background
Accurate non-invasive diagnostic tools are urgently needed for patients with pulmonary nodules detected in CT scans. Blood DNA methylation sequencing data, known for its continuity and stability, offers a promising avenue for developing effective predictive models to classify nodule types.
Methods
DNA methylation sequencing was performed on samples from patients with pulmonary nodules, including both blood and tissue specimens. The dataset was divided as follows: 70% of the blood samples served as the training cohort for model construction, while the remaining 30% of blood samples (test cohort) and all tissue samples (tissue cohort) were used to validate model accuracy. In the training cohort, genes with an average methylation level difference exceeding 5% between malignant and benign groups were identified, then ROC method was employed to filter genes with AUC above 0.65 or below 0.35, and the random forest method was used to build this prediction model. Finally, GSEA and GSVA were employed in DNA methylation data sequencing to elucidate the biological mechanisms underlying the model’s predictive efficacy.
Results
In this study, 187 samples with clearly classified nodules were sequenced, including 154 blood and 33 tissue samples (all enrolled malignant nodules were at early stage). A total of 64 genes were selected using the averaged methylation level filter to perform ROC, and nine genes were used to build the prediction model. The AUC of risk score for this model was 1.00, 0.93, and 0.96 in the training, test, and tissue cohorts, respectively. In the results of GSEA and GSVA, 79.4% (100/126) and 81.0% (102/126) of cell cycle-related pathways were significantly enriched in the low-risk score group, respectively. These findings suggest that lower risk scores correlate with reduced cell cycle activation, which is consistent with the higher proliferative activity observed in malignant nodules.
Conclusions
This study developed a random forest model by DNA methylation sequencing data, demonstrating high predictive accuracy for pulmonary nodule classification. The model's risk score exhibits a positive correlation with the activation of cell cycle-related pathways, highlighting its potential clinical utility in non-invasive diagnosis.

title: 1766eP Deep learning-based digital pathology algorithm overcomes tumor content limitations for FGFR alteration detection in non-muscle invasive bladder cancer
abstract:
Background
Tissue insufficiency may pose a barrier to diagnostic testing in non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC), as tumor volumes in the early disease setting may fall below assay input requirements. This constraint may impact clinical development and future access to FGFR targeted treatments for NMIBC patients. Here, we demonstrate that an AI-based digital pathology algorithm, MIA:BLC-FGFR, using only a single H&E-stained whole slide image (WSI), can accurately detect the presence of FGFR alterations in NMIBC tissue samples where minimum assay tissue requirements were not met.
Methods
We evaluated MIA:BLC-FGFR on 169 WSIs from NMIBC tissue blocks, where FGFR testing was performed using a RT-PCR assay performed on unstained slides from the respective block. Among these blocks, 67% (113/169) required multiple unstained tissue slides from the same block to achieve the required tumor area for analysis, resulting in the use of 518 additional unstained slides. MIA:BLC-FGFR's performance was assessed against varying minimum tumor area thresholds on the WSIs: ≥100 mm2, ≥50 mm2, ≥25 mm2, ≥10 mm2, ≥5 mm2, and ≥1 mm2, with tumor surface area obtained computationally.
Results
MIA:BLC-FGFR performance is shown in the table,

MIA:BLC-FGFR exhibited consistent performance across various tumor areas, with auROC ranging from 87% for tissues with ≥1mm2 to 90% for ≥100mm2. Overall, 243% more slides were needed to obtain FGFR results with the RT-PCR assay compared to MIA:BLC-FGFR, which required only one slide to provide an FGFR result.
Conclusions
MIA:BLC-FGFR effectively detected the presence of FGFR alterations from a single H&E-stained WSI, even in NMIBC tumors, where limited tumor tissue may be available. This advancement may enhance accessibility to therapeutics for NMIBC patients.

title: 1918P DigiNetGPT: Evaluation of a GPT-based conversational ai tool supporting genomic/health literacy in advanced lung cancer within the national Network Genomic Medicine (nNGM, Germany)
abstract:
Background
Patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) are confronted with complex molecular testing results and treatment landscapes. Drawing on patient input, DigiNetGPT was developed to provide personalized responses to patient questions. This study evaluates its clinical utility, technical performance, and impact on patient literacy and decision confidence.

Methods
DigiNetGPT is based on ChatGPT-4 using a clinician-curated corpus of literature and a local trial database. It is conditioned by three-layered prompts—system, safety, and user—live internet access ensures currency. Participants were stratified by age, molecular status and current treatment. A mixed-methods, two-level design was applied. Level 1 assessed technical functionality and perceived usefulness via semi-structured qualitative feedback to guide iterative refinement. Level 2 applied a pre-post survey design based on validated instruments. It assessed the perceived literacy in different domains such as molecular findings, treatment options, side-effects, prognosis, clinical trials, supportive care. Post-survey additions measured usefulness regarding different patient-centred tasks as well as digital-judgement items (trustworthiness, relevance, bias detection). Data on social determinants and digital experience were also recorded.

Results
Data collection is ongoing in a cohort of 200 patients. Preliminary trends indicate increased confidence in interpreting molecular findings and treatment options. Qualitative feedback shows the tool’s clarity, and perceived trustworthiness but also diverging expectations regarding the level of scientific detail—insights that will guide interface personalisation. Final quantitative outcomes and subgroup analyses will be presented.

Conclusions
DigiNet GPT appears to enhance digital health literacy, potentially contributing to quality of life and patient empowerment. Refinement of the tool is ongoing to accommodate e.g. different levels of health literacy at baseline. The findings will shape a forthcoming controlled study of comparative effectiveness against standard educational materials.

title: 182eP Improving breast cancer prognosis: Comparison of a new AI-driven multimodal tool for risk stratification with the 21-gene expression signature in real-world setting
abstract:
Background
Implementation of the 21-gene expression assay (ODX) for early HR+/HER2– breast cancer (BC) has helped with chemotherapy reduction, but many patients (pts) fall into an intermediate-risk category. The Ataraxis Breast model (ATX) is an AI tool integrating digital pathology with clinical data, showing promising results in prognostic accuracy.

Methods
269 HR+/HER2– BC pts treated at Basel University Hospital (2010–2021) with ODX scores and digitized H&E slides were included. The ATX generated a risk score from image-derived and basic clinical features. Primary endpoint was disease free interval (DFI). Our objective was to evaluate overall accuracy of ATX and compare it to ODX, using the concordance (C-) index.

Results
ATX showed robust prognostic performance, with high-risk pts having worse DFI compared to low-risk pts (HR: 2.37, p = 0.032) and showed higher prognostic accuracy (C-index 0.69) than ODX (C-index 0.55). ATX reclassified risk categories: from 60 pts labeled as low risk by the ODX, 20 (33%, 95% CI: 21–46%) were defined high risk by ATX. For pts with an intermediate ODX score (n=167), ATX relabeled 128 (77%, 95% CI: 70–83%) as low risk and 39 (23%, 95% CI: 17–30%) as high risk. Among the 42 pts classified as high risk by ODX, ATX defined 19 (44%, 95% CI: 29–60%) as low risk. In multivariate analysis, ATX achieved more accuracy than ODX (HR=4.18, p<0.001) – see table. Specific clinical and pathological factors were associated with ATX odds for higher risk such as pT2 and pT3 stages (OR = 9.72, p = 0.002, and OR = 25.91, p = 0.021, respectively) age < 50 years (OR = 1.05, p = 0.029) and premenopausal status (OR = 0.45, p = 0.183).

title: 1783eP Epigenomic multicancer detection algorithms capture disease biomarkers through machine learning
abstract:
Background
Liquid biopsy tests based on multianalyte measurements employ machine learning (ML) to identify cancer-specific biomarkers. Multicancer detection (MCD) tests are trained to recognize biomarker patterns that are shared by many cancers as well as those unique to each cancer type, enabling them to accurately detect cancer and pinpoint its tissue of origin (TOO). Here, we developed a MCD test based on a diverse panel of cancer cohort using ML to predict TOO, which discovered biological features that reflect known disease biology.

Methods
The training set consisted of 859 cancer (Breast ER-negative, CRC, Esophageal, Gastric, Liver, Lung, Ovarian and Pancreatic) and 1,110 non-cancer patients for which 5hmC, CNV and fragmentation features were available. Cancer detection model was trained with 10-fold cross-validation and separately a TOO model was built to distinguish among 8 cancer types. Model features were extracted and mapped to hg38 genes. MSigDB collections and PantherDB pathways were used for functional annotation.

Results
UV_RESPONSE_DN and MITOTIC_SPINDLE pathways are the top enriched Hallmark pathways by cancer detection model features, as well as several oncogenic pathways (C6). The pathways are significantly associated with cellular changes prior or during cancer development. 37% immunologic signature gene sets (C7) are significantly enriched by cancer detection model features, T cell (CD4, CD8, TREG) genesets are among the top enriched sets. For TOO model features, we found tissue cell-specific genesets are significantly enriched by corresponding model features. For example, liver and pancreatic gene sets are enriched in model features specific to liver and pancreatic respectively.

Conclusions
Hallmark pathways enrichment in MCD cancer detection model suggest oncogenic transformation underlied by dysregulated cell division and breakdown of genomic integrity. Immunogenic pathways enrichment suggests the model features also capture anti-tumor immune responses. MCD TOO model features show strong enrichment in cell type–specific gene sets corresponding to the corresponding tissue, indicating that ML captures signals of relevant transcriptional programs.

title: 2047eP Performance of large language models in multidisciplinary planning for lung-cancer brain metastases
abstract:
Background
Multidisciplinary tumour boards (MTBs) improve outcomes in lung-cancer brain metastases, yet many hospitals cannot convene all specialties or track rapidly expanding evidence. Large language models (LLMs) could synthesise guidelines and patient data to support MTB decisions.

Methods
Six virtual cases covering varied histology, molecular status (EGFR, ALK, KRAS, PD-L1) and intracranial patterns (solitary, multiple, leptomeningeal) were created. GPT-4o (OpenAI) and DeepSeek-R1 each received a standard prompt emulating an MTB agenda with four roles: medical oncology, thoracic surgery, neurosurgery and radiation oncology. A blinded four-member specialist panel scored every output on accuracy, comprehensiveness, clarity, personalisation, hallucination control and ethical safety (1–5 Likert). Means were compared with two-sided t tests (α = 0.05).

Results
Across 24 model–case pairs, the overall mean score was 3.79 ± 1.03. Both hallucination control and ethical safety exceeded 4.0, indicating low risk of harmful content. DeepSeek-R1 outperformed GPT-4o in composite quality (4.14 ± 0.88 vs 3.44 ± 1.06; P<0.001) and in accuracy (4.13 vs 3.17; P<0.001), comprehensiveness (4.13 vs 3.08; P<0.001) and personalisation (3.63 vs 2.83; P=0.019). Differences in clarity and safety domains were non-significant. DeepSeek scored higher in medical oncology, thoracic surgery and radiation oncology (all P≤0.01), with parity in neurosurgery. GPT-4o surpassed DeepSeek only in an ALK-positive case where DeepSeek’s lengthy plan lacked focus.

Conclusions
GPT-4o and DeepSeek-R1 generated MTB-style recommendations of acceptable quality for lung-cancer brain metastases; DeepSeek showed superior accuracy and breadth. High safety and low hallucination scores support exploratory clinical use. Future work should pair structured prompts with retrieval-augmented generation and multimodal inputs to optimise LLM support for complex oncology decisions.

title: 3202eP MRI-based radiomics for prediction of epidermal growth factor receptor in glioma through artificial intelligence models: A systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract:
Background
Gliomas are the most common primary brain malignancies in adults. Lower-grade gliomas and the response to treatment and survival of these patients differ significantly due to genetic differences between lower-grade gliomas. Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is a key glioma molecular biomarker and is known to promote increased proliferation of tumour cells. Radiomic imaging techniques extract quantitative features from medical images like MRI and CT scans with the help of advanced algorithms and the extracted data can be utilized in the development of specific artificial intelligence (AI) models like Neural Networks for the prediction of presence of EGFR. EGFR-targeted drug therapy is known to have a better prognosis in low-grade gliomas. The meta-analysis aims to assess the diagnostic potential of Radiomic imaging in detecting EGFR.

Methods
A systematic search was conducted using PubMed, Google Scholar, and Scopus. PRISMA guidelines were followed. A boolean expression was constructed to retrieve and select articles from major medical databases. The R Studio package was used to evaluate the potential of the diagnostic test. The Pooled sensitivity and specificity were estimated to predict the diagnostic potential of Radiomic Imaging in detecting EGFR mutations in gliomas. The random effects model via the linear (mixed-effects) model framework was considered for statistical analysis.

Results
A total of 7 studies with 523 observations were assessed through this meta-analysis. The Pooled Sensitivity and Specificity were estimated to be 77.70% ([67.85; 87.51], 95% CI, p< 0.0001, z = 15.418, SE = 0.05) and 84.75% ([79.12; 88.7], 95% CI, p<0.0001, z = 34.53, SE = 0.02) utilising the random effects model.

Conclusions
MRI-based Radiomics show pooled Sensitivity of 77.70% and High Pooled Specificity of 84.75% in detecting EGFR mutations in Glioblastoma. MRI-based Radiomics is a dependable and consistent non-invasive technique in the detection of EGFR mutations in Gliomas. It can be utilised for the generation of predictive models, enhancing clinical diagnosis and tailored management based on EGFR mutation.

title: Clinical validation of a tissue-agnostic genome-wide methylome enrichment molecular residual disease assay for head and neck malignancies
abstract: BACKGROUND: Outcomes for patients with locally advanced head and neck cancer (HNC) treated with curative intent remain disappointing, with 5-year survival rates at 50%. Most recurrences occur within the first 2 years after treatment, providing a window of opportunity to identify patients with molecular residual disease (MRD). A tissue-agnostic test for MRD detection in patients with human papillomavirus (HPV) positive and negative HNC, where tissue is often scarce, is needed. PATIENTS AND METHODS: Patients with stage I-IVB HNC, including patients positive and negative for HPV, were enrolled and peripheral blood plasma was collected longitudinally at diagnosis and ∼3, 12, and 24 months after curative intent treatment. The full cohort includes 325 patients with 1155 samples. Samples were split into distinct sets to train and validate a classifier capable of identifying MRD using a tissue-agnostic genome-wide methylome enrichment platform. The primary endpoint was recurrence-free survival (RFS). RESULTS: With a median follow-up of 60 months, patients in the blinded validation set with MRD positivity experienced significantly worse RFS with a hazard ratio (HR) of 35.7 [95% confidence interval (CI) 10.8-117.8; P < 0.0001]. For patients with HPV negativity, HR was 42.3 (95% CI 9.8-182.3; P < 0.0001); for patients with HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer, HR was 24.1 (95% CI 3.0-196.8; P < 0.0001). Moreover, the lead time between MRD positivity and clinical recurrence was up to 14.9 months, with a mean lead time of 4.1 months. Surveillance sensitivity was 91% (95% CI 77% to 97%) and specificity was 88% (95% CI 80% to 93%). CONCLUSIONS: Here we validate the clinical performance characteristics of a tissue-agnostic genome-wide methylome enrichment assay for MRD detection in patients with HNC. The MRD detection test showed high sensitivity for identifying recurrence at high specificity across different anatomical sites, HPV status, and treatment regimens, highlighting the broad applicability for MRD detection in patients with HNC.

title: Enhanced risk stratification for stage II colorectal cancer using deep learning-based CT classifier and pathological markers to optimize adjuvant therapy decision
abstract: BACKGROUND: Current risk stratification for stage II colorectal cancer (CRC) has limited accuracy in identifying patients who would benefit from adjuvant chemotherapy, leading to potential overtreatment or undertreatment. We aimed to develop a more precise risk stratification system by integrating artificial intelligence-based imaging analysis with pathological markers. PATIENTS AND METHODS: We analyzed 2992 stage II CRC patients from 12 centers. A deep learning classifier (Swin Transformer Assisted Risk-stratification for CRC, STAR-CRC) was developed using multi-planar computed tomography (CT) images from 1587 patients (training : internal validation = 7 : 3) and validated in 1405 patients from eight independent centers, which stratified patients into low-, uncertain-, and high-risk groups. To further refine the uncertain-risk group, a composite score based on pathological markers (pT4 stage, number of lymph nodes sampled, perineural invasion, and lymphovascular invasion) was applied, forming the Intelligent Risk Integration System for stage II Colorectal Cancer (IRIS-CRC). IRIS-CRC was compared against the guideline-based risk stratification system (GRSS-CRC) for prediction performance and validated in the validation dataset. RESULTS: IRIS-CRC stratified patients into four prognostic groups with distinct 3-year disease-free survival rates (≥95%, 95%-75%, 75%-55%, ≤55%). Upon external validation, compared with GRSS-CRC, IRIS-CRC downstaged 27.1% of high-risk patients into the favorable group, and upstaged 6.5% of low-risk patients into the very poor prognosis group who might require more aggressive treatment. In the GRSS-CRC intermediate-risk group of the external validation dataset, IRIS-CRC reclassified 40.1% as favorable prognosis and 7.0% as very poor prognosis. IRIS-CRC's performance maintained generalizability in both chemotherapy and non-chemotherapy cohorts. CONCLUSIONS: IRIS-CRC offers a more precise and personalized risk assessment than current guideline-based risk factors, potentially sparing low-risk patients from unnecessary adjuvant chemotherapy while identifying high-risk individuals for more aggressive treatment. This novel approach holds promise for improving clinical decision-making and outcomes in stage II CRC.
